questions.explanation: 'Suggests' hedges the claim, presenting it as interpretation rather than proven fact.
questions.q: Choose the appropriately hedged academic claim.

questions.explanation: 'May' as a modal hedge softens the assertion to a possibility.
questions.q: These findings ___ indicate a broader trend.

questions.explanation: Academic stance avoids overclaiming; 'appear to' hedges the observation.
The tentative 'it is possible that' hedges more than the categorical alternatives.
The passive 'it has been argued' distances the writer from the claim, a classic hedge.
Limiting adverbs like 'to some extent' qualify the scope of the claim.
'Seems' hedges the evaluation, marking it as the writer's reading of the evidence.
questions.q: This ___ an oversimplification of a complex issue.

questions.explanation: Reporting verbs like 'claim' signal that the view belongs to others, not the writer.
questions.q: Critics ___ that the reforms have failed.

questions.explanation: The modal 'could' hedges the causal explanation as one possibility among others.
'Tend to' hedges a generalisation, avoiding an absolute statement.
'Somewhat' downtoners soften evaluative adjectives in academic prose.
The impersonal 'there is some evidence' hedges the strength of support.
'Would appear' is a double hedge marking the conclusion as tentative.
'Albeit limited' concedes weakness while maintaining the stance, a nuanced hedge.
questions.q: The study offers ___, support for the model.

questions.explanation: Boosters like 'clearly' strengthen stance; here the task needs the tentative form.
questions.q: This is ___ the most significant finding.

questions.explanation: 'Cannot be ruled out' hedges by keeping an alternative explanation open.
The passive reporting structure distances the writer from the asserted view.
'In all likelihood' expresses high probability while stopping short of certainty.
'Raises the possibility' hedges the inference as speculative rather than established.
questions.q: This ___ that other factors are involved.

questions.explanation: The concessive 'while' clause acknowledges limits before stating the stance.
options: While the sample is small, the pattern is striking
The sample is perfect and proves everything
Small samples always prove the point
The pattern is certain despite no data
